name: Phase Four: The Six Week Pilot
title: Phase Four: The Six Week Pilot
answer: The Six Week Pilot is the fourth phase of a school's adoption process, in which two or three volunteer teachers use a tool as designed for six weeks while tracking one main measure recorded before and after. It matters because six weeks is long enough to reveal a pattern and short enough to stop without regret, and it ends with a decision meeting scheduled before the pilot even starts.

sections.body: This idea is a bounded trial that a school or district runs before committing to a tool more widely. It solves the problem of adopting something on enthusiasm alone, because a short, structured pilot produces a written result that people can examine before deciding whether they liked the tool. The pilot uses two or three teachers who volunteered, asks them to use the tool as designed, and asks them to report honestly. It tracks a single main measure, taken before the tool arrives and again at the end. A decision meeting closes the pilot on a date that was set before the pilot began.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school, the pilot runs for six weeks with two or three volunteer teachers, one main measure recorded at the start and again at the end, and a decision meeting already on the calendar. Choosing the teachers takes thought: volunteers make things run smoothly, but a group made only of the most enthusiastic users says little about how the tool works for everyone else, so including at least one curious but skeptical teacher makes the results more believable and helps surface problems enthusiasts miss. Where possible, the school compares three classrooms using the tool with three similar classrooms that do not, which helps show whether a change came from the tool or from something else such as the time of year. When no comparison group is possible, the baseline measure has to carry more of the weight. For any tool students use to practice, the pilot also needs a check done without the tool, such as a short paper quiz, a conversation, or a task completed without AI, because practice scores can rise while real learning falls. Figure 4.5 lays out the six week template.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure or finding for this idea beyond the reference to Figure 4.5, which lays out the six week template, and the point carried over from Chapter 1 that practice scores can rise while real learning falls. It offers no evidence label, so this idea rests on practice rather than research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are built into the design. Six weeks is deliberately short so a school can stop without regret, and the results should be written down before anyone decides whether they liked the tool, which keeps the decision from turning on enthusiasm. A pilot staffed only by the most enthusiastic users will tell the district little about how the tool works for everyone else, so at least one curious but skeptical teacher belongs in the group. Where a comparison group is not possible, the baseline has to carry more of the weight, and the district should read the result with that in mind. For tools students use to practice, a check done without the tool is required, because a rise in practice scores alone does not show that learning happened. The decision itself stays with the people in the decision meeting.
